title: Bomber Command Museum of Canada
summary: The small-town Alberta museum with a flying Lancaster bomber - one of only two airworthy Lancasters in the world, restored by volunteers in a prairie town of 2,000 where the plane was kept as a memorial since 1960.

content.intro: In Nanton, Alberta, population 2,000, a Lancaster bomber roars to life. The FM159 is one of only two airworthy Lancaster bombers remaining in the world - the aircraft that carried the weight of Bomber Command's offensive against Nazi Germany. This particular Lancaster never saw combat; it arrived in Canada too late for the war. But it was preserved as a memorial in Nanton beginning in 1960, sitting outdoors on the prairie, gradually deteriorating. In 1986, volunteers formed a restoration group. Over the next decades, they brought the Lancaster back to flying condition - not just taxiing, but actually flying, though only rarely due to maintenance costs. The Bomber Command Museum now houses the Lancaster and a collection of other WWII aircraft, engines, and memorabilia. It's an improbable treasure in an improbable place, saved by small-town determination.

sections.title: The Lancaster
sections.body: The Avro Lancaster was Britain's primary heavy bomber during World War II. Over 7,300 were built; Lancasters flew over 156,000 sorties, dropping 608,000 tons of bombs. They attacked German industry, cities, and infrastructure - controversial then and now, but decisive. The Lancaster was versatile: it carried the 'Upkeep' bouncing bomb for the Dam Busters raid and the 22,000-pound 'Grand Slam' earthquake bomb. Of the thousands built, only seventeen complete Lancasters survive today. Only two are airworthy: FM159 in Nanton and PA474 in Britain. The Lancaster is an icon of WWII aviation, and Nanton's is flying.

sections.title: The Preservation
sections.body: FM159 was built in 1945, too late for combat. It served as a maritime patrol aircraft and aerial survey platform before being retired in 1960. The town of Nanton acquired it as a memorial, displaying it outdoors on concrete pads. For 25 years, weather and neglect took their toll. By 1985, the airframe was deteriorating badly. Local volunteers formed the Nanton Lancaster Society and began restoration. Working weekends and evenings, they rebuilt the aircraft piece by piece. In 2003, FM159 ran its engines for the first time in decades. In 2013, it taxied under its own power. Today, it flies occasionally - brief demonstration flights that draw crowds from across Canada.

sections.title: The Museum
sections.body: The Bomber Command Museum of Canada grew around the Lancaster restoration. The hangar houses not just FM159 but a collection of WWII aircraft, including a Mosquito (under restoration), engines, turrets, and bombs. Exhibits tell the story of Bomber Command - the campaign, the crews, the controversies. Personal artifacts from veterans fill display cases. The museum is professionally curated despite its volunteer origins. Over 40,000 visitors come annually to a town of 2,000, drawn by the Lancaster and the dedication that saved it. The museum has become Nanton's primary attraction, a testament to what volunteers can accomplish.

sections.title: The Controversy
sections.body: Bomber Command's campaign against Germany remains controversial. The strategic bombing offensive killed hundreds of thousands of German civilians, including the firebombing of Dresden that killed up to 25,000. Defenders argue the campaign shortened the war and diverted German resources from other fronts; critics call it terror bombing. The museum addresses this complexity, presenting the campaign's history without simple judgments. The Lancaster itself is neither hero nor villain - it's a machine that did what its crews were ordered to do. The museum honors those crews, 55,573 of whom died, while acknowledging the suffering their missions caused.

sections.title: Visiting the Bomber Command Museum
sections.body: The Bomber Command Museum of Canada is located at 1729 21st Avenue in Nanton, Alberta, on Highway 2 about 70 kilometers south of Calgary. The museum is open daily from May through October, with limited winter hours. Admission is charged. The Lancaster ground runs occur on special occasions; check the schedule for dates. The museum has a gift shop and café. Nanton is a small town with limited services; Calgary has full amenities. Calgary International Airport is 70 kilometers north. The drive from Calgary passes through Alberta foothills with views of the Rocky Mountains to the west. Allow at least 2-3 hours for the museum.

content.flightContext: Located at 50.35°N, 113.77°W in Nanton, Alberta, on the eastern edge of the Canadian foothills. From altitude, Nanton is a small town grid along Highway 2, with the museum hangar visible on the western edge of town. The Rocky Mountains rise dramatically to the west. Calgary is 70 kilometers north. The terrain transitions from prairie to foothills - rolling grassland giving way to forested ridges. The Lancaster, if outside, may be visible on the apron. Calgary International Airport is the nearest major commercial service.
